meta.title: Who really said "Love makes your soul crawl out from its hiding place"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Zora Neale Hurston wrote a version of this line in Their Eyes Were Watching God (1937), but the popular aphorism is a paraphrase of her actual sentence about Janie.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Love makes your soul crawl out from its hiding place'?
meta.ogDescription: Hurston really wrote it — but as "So her soul crawled out from its hiding place" about Janie in Their Eyes Were Watching God (1937). The maxim is a paraphrase.

answer.label: Not quite Hurston’s words — a paraphrase of her novel
answer.sourceLine: The imagery is genuinely Hurston’s, but the popular wording is a paraphrase. In ‘Their Eyes Were Watching God’ (1937, ch. 13) she wrote of Janie: “…felt a self-crushing love. So her soul crawled out from its hiding place.” The free-standing maxim “Love makes your soul crawl out from its hiding place” is a later, generalized rewording that does not appear verbatim in her work.

source.heading: Where the line really comes from
source.excerpt: He drifted off into sleep and Janie looked down on him and felt a self-crushing love. So her soul crawled out from its hiding place.
trail: The popular maxim “Love makes your soul crawl out from its hiding place” is shared everywhere with no source; Goodreads lists it under Hurston with no book cited.
Attribution reviewers at WIST Quotations checked ‘Their Eyes Were Watching God’ and could not find the maxim there, downgrading it to “(Attributed).”
The real line appears at the close of Chapter 13: “So her soul crawled out from its hiding place” — describing Janie, not love in the abstract.
source.excerptNote: Hurston’s actual sentence — a specific narrative moment about Janie and Tea Cake, not the general maxim that circulates online.

author.name: Zora Neale Hurston
author.heading: About the author
author.bio: Zora Neale Hurston (1891–1960) was a novelist, anthropologist and folklorist central to the Harlem Renaissance. Her best-known novel, Their Eyes Were Watching God (1937), follows Janie Crawford’s search for love and selfhood in rural Florida. Hurston trained in anthropology under Franz Boas and wove Black Southern vernacular and folklore through her fiction.

misattribution.heading: The wording problem
misattribution.intro: This is not a fabrication pinned on a famous name — the imagery is truly Hurston’s. What circulates online is a paraphrase: her specific sentence about a character has been smoothed into a universal maxim she never actually wrote.

items.why: The aphorism “Love makes your soul crawl out from its hiding place” does not appear in any known Hurston text. She wrote a narrative sentence about Janie—“felt a self-crushing love. So her soul crawled out from its hiding place”—which quote collections later rephrased into a free-standing motto.

items.who: Their Eyes Were Watching God, ch. 13
items.why: Sites that do name a source point to Chapter 13 of the 1937 novel, but the actual passage reads differently from the popular version and describes Janie rather than love in general.

misattribution.truthLine: Hurston really wrote the image—“So her soul crawled out from its hiding place”—but the tidy maxim making the rounds is a later rewording, not her sentence.

context.heading: What she actually wrote
lead: In Chapter 13 of ‘Their Eyes Were Watching God,’ Janie has just been through a night of fear over Tea Cake—he vanished with her savings, then returned having won it all back. Watching him sleep, she feels “a self-crushing love,” and Hurston writes: “So her soul crawled out from its hiding place.”

The line is a turning point: after two guarded marriages, Janie’s guarded inner self finally emerges. The personification—a soul that had been in hiding, now venturing out—is precise and character-specific, which is exactly why the flattened maxim loses something in translation.
